A Robust Co-training Framework to Handle Noisy
Labels for Remote Sensing Image Segmentation
Mitsuyoshi Otsu, Member, IEEE, Jun Zhou, Senior Member, IEEE, Bo Han, Arnon Accad, Shirui Pan
Abstract—Effective learning with noisy labels is crucial in
remote sensing data analysis, not only for instance-wise prediction
but also for pixel-wise prediction. The recent surge in demand
for robust machine learning models emphasizes the necessity
of constructing large datasets and managing associated costs
carefully. This trend highlights the potential of utilizing coarsely
annotated datasets, which commonly entail the risk of producing
noisy labels. To address label noise, methods of learning with
noisy labels have been proposed for instance-wise classification
assessed in computer vision. However, previous studies have
not provided a detailed discussion on how to detect human
error at the pixel level and how to adapt the resulting error
maps within a single end-to-end learning framework in remote
sensing. To address these issues, we propose a new co-training
framework for segmentation modeling with automatic filtering
to reduce the negative effects caused by noisy labels in the
training dataset. Our method has three key contributions: (1)
a trainable filter module to identify uncertain pixels at each
iteration, (2) a weighted multi-loss strategy to effectively filter
out uncertain training loss, and (3) a collaborative filter update
based on outputs from co-trained networks. To assess the
effectiveness of our method, we conducted experiments on the
DeepGlobe landcover classification dataset, a self-constructed
mangrove dataset, and the Massachusetts building dataset. We
compared the performance of our method to several state-of-
the-art noise-robust methods. The experimental results reveal
that our proposed method outperforms the alternatives and
demonstrates greater effectiveness on multi-class segmentation
tasks.
Index Terms—Deep learning, noisy labels, semantic segmenta-
tion, co-training, multi-class classification, remote sensing.
I. INTRODUCTION
While Deep Learning (DL) in remote sensing data analysis
has emerged as a cornerstone technique with significant ex-
pectations for practical usage such as agriculture [1], forestry
[2] and urban planning [3]. The rapid increase in demand of
DL has lifted the model’s capacity in high-accuracy prediction
and promoted careful cost management for annotation to
create large datasets. This trend has led to the proliferation of
experimental datasets, but it has also introduced the potential
risk of noisy labels due to the trade-off between the qual-
ity and quantity of datasets, which can commonly degrade
the model’s performance significantly. The causes of label
noise can be roughly categorized into two factors: coarse
annotation through automatic processing or crowd-sourcing,

intraclass diversity and interclass similarity in remote sensing
imagery. The first factor is due to the high demand for low-
cost data creation methods that introduce noises into labels,
which is similar to that in general classification tasks [4]. In
handling this challenging factor, one-by-one data cleansing for
corrupted labels is impractical [5], and standard regulariza-
tion techniques cannot completely solve this issue [4], [6].
Therefore, it is a critical task to develop robust learning with
coarsely annotated datasets [7]–[12]. On the other hand, the
difficulty in annotation is more specific to remote sensing
data analysis, making human annotation a challenging task.
Many studies have tried to mitigate the negative effects of
this challenge in various kinds of projects, e.g. satellite and
UAV image vegetation analysis [13]–[17], road and building
detection [18], [19], multi-label image classification [20],
and hyperspectral image classification [5]. These two non-
negligible factors are sensational to the development of high-
quality DL models without the high-cost requirement of plenty
of expert annotations.
Handling noisy labels has become one of the key tasks in
robust deep learning. Due to the unsatisfactory results of stan-
dard regularization methods such as data augmentation, weight
decay, dropout, and batch normalization [4], there has emerged
a need to develop new learning paradigms optimized for robust
learning with noisy labels. The initial approach to address
this need was based on fine-tuning techniques, but it was
found to exhibit lower accuracy compared to models trained
from scratch with clean and massively noisy labels [21]. As a
consequence, the research spotlight shifted to efficient training
with single datasets, not considering being given clean and
noisy datasets separately. As the next step, some research
focused on the estimation of the latent transition matrix of
labels. Patrini et al. [22] introduced an easy way to approx-
imate it using simple datasets with synthetic noisy labels.
However, it is also pointed out that real noise contains more
randomness and complex patterns than synthetic ones, making
it difficult to incorporate the latent transition matrix into more
complex situations [23]–[25], especially when dealing with a
large number of classes [10]. Moreover, many methods were
proposed based on various types of techniques such as robust
network architecture [26], prominent loss functions [27], meta-
learning [28], and metric learning [29], [30]. But the most
popular and promising one seems to be data selection [9]–
[12], which eliminates uncertain samples with a relatively high
loss function, considered as noisy ones, from datasets during
training. For instance, MentorNet [9] and Co-teaching [10]
adopt a collaborative learning approach with two networks

Despite various studies on learning with noisy labels in
image classification, few studies are addressing noisy pixels
in label masks for semantic segmentation. Whereas previous
image classification methods often assume that labels can
be classified as either clean or noisy, most label masks in
semantic segmentation contain a mix of clean and noisy pixel
information, making it difficult to categorize them without
arbitrary decision-making. For instance, in Fig. 1, we show
a sample from a segmentation dataset where the presence of a
river is not reflected in the label map. In this example, since the
noisy pixels appear limited in number, the instance-level dis-
tribution of loss may be too similar to that of cleaner samples,
making effective sample selection challenging. Moreover, in
general, the configuration of polygons in segmentation datasets
inevitably includes mislabeled boundaries between different
categories, as annotation is typically not done pixel-by-pixel,
making the definition of a “clean sample” ambiguous. Due to
the ambiguity, training models with noisy labels in semantic
segmentation is closely related to the research field of Weakly
Supervised Semantic Segmentation (WSSS), where weaker
forms of supervision like image-level labels or bounding
boxes are used for model training. Some studies in WSSS
discuss methods for reducing noisy information from various
perspectives, such as early learning [31], co-training [32], and
joint loss functions [33]. However, these studies primarily
focus on effectively training models with weaker supervision,
and it is challenging to directly generalize these methods to
other types of noisy labels. Although other studies explore
various ideas, such as combining label correction and sam-
ple reweighting [34], utilizing data with different resolutions
simultaneously [35], and adapting WSSS methods to more
specialized fields [36], fundamental schemes for noise-robust
learning in semantic segmentation with strong generalization
abilities to adapt to datasets across various research fields have
not been established.
In this study, we propose a novel co-training learning frame-
work to mitigate the negative effects of noisy pixels in multi-
class semantic segmentation for remote sensing data analysis,
focusing on detecting noise and leveraging the detected infor-
mation to enhance network training. A co-training framework
is widely used for sample selection, weakly supervised seman-
tic segmentation (WSSS), and other tasks aimed at reducing
error accumulation in a single network [10], [32], [37], [38].
Due to the scarcity of studies on this topic, our framework
leverages effective WSSS methods and integrates them into a
unified model tailored for remote sensing applications. In our
method, we incorporate filtering masks that capture uncertainty
information in pixel-wise label maps, enabling the model to
account for spatial characteristics and label ambiguity inherent
in semantic segmentation datasets. Our approach comprises
three key technical components:
1) Trainable filtering Masks: We introduce a dynamic fil-
tering module that generates per-batch updated filtering
masks. This approach helps avoid excessive learning in

2) Weighted multi-Loss strategy: We propose a novel
weighted multi-loss format in which the filtering masks
are computed to serve as effective weights for the loss
functions. Additionally, we integrate CRF-Loss into our
weighted multi-loss scheme to mitigate information loss,
thereby preserving the spatial context of the source
images in the predicted maps [33], drawing inspiration
from CRF-based post-processing techniques [39].
3) Collaborative refinement of filtering module: We
introduce a novel co-training Framework in which co-
trained networks not only share noisy information but
also provide inputs to the filtering module, thereby facili-
tating the learning of consensus error regions throughout
the training process.
To validate the effectiveness of our method, we conducted
experiments with three types of datasets: the DeepGlobe
land cover classification dataset, a self-constructed Mangrove
detection dataset, and the Massachusetts building footprint
segmentation dataset. We conducted model training with previ-
ous methods, including SFL [19] and AIO2 [40] which shows
the effectiveness for noisy binary classification but has yet to
adapt to multi-class ones.
The article is organized as follows: Section II summarizes
related studies on learning methodologies with noisy labels.
Technical details of the proposed method are described in
Section III. Next, we discuss the experimental results from two
perspectives: network dependency and comparison to other
methods in Section IV. This is followed by an elaboration
of the results in Section V and ablation studies in Section VI,
and we conclude this work with future lines in Section VII.
II. RELATED WORK
A. Learning with Noisy Label for Image Classification
Due to the unsatisfactory reliability of automatically col-
lected labels, many studies in image classification have fo-
cused on how to conduct robust learning with noisy annotated
data. The recent trend of large capacity models for obtaining

to noisy labels due to the memorization effect [9], which

noise transition matrix, which shows all probabilities of label

Nevertheless, real-world noise is caused in a more complex
scenario, especially when the class number is large [10], [23],
[25]. While many robust methods to handle noisy labels have
been proposed from various approaches, the least task-specific
approach seems to be sample selection because of the simple
strategy that selects and eliminates noisy labels from datasets
by referring to uncertainty calculated from model output and
labels during training [4]. MentorNet [9] uses an additional
network providing meaningful supervision not to cause serious
memorization of the training model to noisy labels by referring
to the Curriculum Learning (CL) scheme. This method adopts
the small-loss trick that selects samples with low losses under
the threshold in each batch operation, regarding them as clean
samples, and uses only selected samples for backpropagation
(self-paced MentorNet). Despite achieving success in some
experiments, it has been pointed out that this method may lead
to error accumulation, as the selective information of uncertain
samples in one network will be directly transferred back to
itself in the next batch calculation [10]. Co-teaching [10]
addresses this drawback by using two networks with the same
structure along the co-training scheme, which is a common
technique for the compensation of crucial information to each
other and reducing the risk of favoring the samples in a single
network [10], [37], [38], [41]. In Co-teaching, each of the
two networks has its parameters and can extract different
types of features from each other, which enables them to
filter out various errors introduced by noisy labels. From a
different perspective, the multi-round learning approach [11],
[12] iteratively selects a set of clean samples by repeating
training rounds without the necessity of training two networks
with the same structure. Overall, many methods following the
sample selection scheme have demonstrated effectiveness for
handling noisy labels, but it’s worth noting that they may suffer
from incorrect selection when the loss distributions of true-
labeled and false-labeled samples overlap significantly [4].
B. Weakly Supervised Semantic Segmentation
Learning with noisy labels can be regarded as one of the
weakly supervised learning problems, so it is meaningful to
search for adaptive technical approaches within the field of
WSSS. In WSSS, pseudo-label masks generated from class ac-
tivation maps are usually used for training segmentation mod-
els, instead of manually annotated ones, after the production
process of well-qualified class activation maps using instance-
wise annotated datasets. In most cases, research in WSSS
focuses on how to produce high-quality masks in the first label
creation stage, but some studies also discuss the quality of
training in the second learning stage with noisy labels, which
originates from the unreliability of weakly annotated datasets.
Li et al. [42] notes the scarcity of specific learning methods in
the second stage and proposes a filtering operation to loss maps
conducted by the multiplication of weight masks referring to
uncertainty on the pixels. From a different viewpoint, ADELE
[31] introduces “early learning” in noisy label learning, which
monitors the process of evaluation index for each category
to find the beginning point of overfitting and stop learning on
the class, and starts pixel-wise label correction if the index has
already saturated. This idea is also used in building segmenta-
tion [40]. As a similar approach to image classification, Rong
et al. [32] adopts the co-training framework in the WSSS,
like Co-teaching [10], and incorporates a boundary-enhanced
strategy to boost predictions on difficult boundary areas. From
the perspective of compensating for uncertain pixels, some
studies pay attention to the unique idea of Conditional Random
Field (CRF), commonly used for post-processing in semantic
segmentation [39], which can refine the shape of predicted
objects by considering relationships such as similarity and
location between pixels in raw images, and introduce advanced
loss functions [33], [36], [43]. Overall, some studies in WSSS
have demonstrated significant insights, but their scope does not
fully account for real-world noise caused by human annotators.
Direct adaptation to remote sensing modelling is challenging
due to the diverse causes of label noise resulting from human
annotation, as highlighted by Liu et al [40].
C. Learning with Noisy Label in Remote Sensing Data Anal-
ysis
Regarding remote sensing data analysis, label noise sig-
nificantly affects model performance. Several studies have
addressed this issue in image classification projects, driven
by the high demand for coarsely annotated data, which is
often produced by crowdsource procedures or publicly avail-
able thematic products [44], [45]. Instinctively, it may seem
reasonable to follow general approaches in computer vision
to tackle this issue, but it has been noted that specific causes
of noise in multi-label scene classification on remote sensing
images necessitate the development of methods optimized
for the remote sensing field [20], [46], which motivated the
development of many methods for various tasks [6], [29], [47].
In semantic segmentation, enhancing robustness to noisy
labels becomes much harder than in image classification
because of its spatial aspect. The common causes of noisy
labels can be categorized into two cases: coarse annotation via
crowdsourcing or automated annotation processes, and hard
annotation requiring a high level of expertise. While the former
aims to reduce annotation costs, the latter originates from the
intrinsic difficulty of remote sensing data analysis. Even in
the same area, multiple remote sensing images captured at
different times can exhibit spectral differences due to seasonal
changes and weather conditions. Despite its significant influ-
ence on model performance, only a few studies have focused
on the topic of noisy learning in semantic segmentation [19],
[35], [40]. Dong et al. [35] conducted an experiment on how to
effectively train models with noisy datasets by combining the
low-resolution landcover product (10m) and high-resolution
satellite images (3m) captured in China, proposing an online
noise correction framework consisting of an uncertainty esti-
mation module and an adaptive correction module. Song el

III. METHODOLOGY
Following previous approaches in image classification, we
leverage the co-training framework [10], [32] to achieve robust
learning despite noisy labels. Because our method is designed
for multi-class segmentation tasks, which are significantly
more complex than image classification, we introduce a novel
co-training framework tailored to these challenges, taking into
account the spatial aspect of labels within a single map. To
address this challenging task, we introduce three modules: the
Mask Production Module (MPM), the Noise Label Production
Module (NLPM), and the Loss-Filtering Module (LFM), each
specifically tailored to our purpose. In this article, a scalar is
denoted by a lowercase letter, e.g., y ∈R. A matrix, denoted
by a bold capital letter, e.g., Y ∈RI×J, has components Yij,
where i = 1, 2, . . . , I and j = 1, 2, . . . , J. A tensor is repre-
sented by a bold calligraphic letter, e.g., Y ∈RI1×I2×···×IN .
Here, we use matrix form when representing 2D maps, even
where each pixel is assigned a specific index in a 1D for-
mat, aligning with intuitive understanding. In the following,
Section III-A provides a brief introduction to pixel-wise co-
training, and Section III-B shows the base framework of our
method. The MPM and NLPM are discussed in Section III-C,
and the process of filtering the loss function in the LFM is
introduced in Section III-D.

co-training framework to train models on datasets containing
uncertain samples, which include both noisy and excessively
difficult ones, thereby suppressing the risk of error accumu-

this framework with a “small-loss trick” [9] where only the
samples with low loss values are selected for updating models,
which is widely used in image classification to handle noisy

lection process should be reformulated as a filtering procedure
applied to the loss maps on the opposite side [49] due to the
2D format of labels, where the loss value of uncertain pixels
is forced to be zero. This leads to the definition of the Masked

inevitably contains ambiguous labels, especially in boundary
regions. Secondly, the training process contains the risk of
causing unstable learning because each pixel also contributes
to constructing a single map with complex spatial information;
excessive filtering may result in fragmented masks lacking
sufficient detailed spatial information.

C. Mask production process

perform noise detection and generate appropriate masks to
enhance network updates. As demonstrated in Equations (4)-
(7), MPM learns parameters to generate suitable mask values
for filtering the loss map on the opposite side, with training fa-
cilitated by sample masks computed from NLPM. This unique
structure can be understood as an additional collaborative
learning mechanism as shown in Fig. 2, where predictions

Additionally, the collaborative framework is expected to
automate the warm-up process [10]. The warm-up process is
a technique that limits loss reduction until the networks have
been trained sufficiently to produce reliable outputs, thereby
ensuring reasonable information selection. In this collaborative
process, the MPM is trained to detect only the predictable
errors in each network in an alternative manner while pre-
serving individual learning. During the initial learning stage,
the NLPM may not produce meaningful sample masks due
to limited accuracy in the co-trained network, resulting in
low-confidence filtering masks in the MPM. In contrast, once
the networks have achieved reasonable accuracy, the MPM
extracts patterns from pairs of network outputs and label maps,
generating filtering masks with higher confidence values and
effectively filtering out noisy or overly challenging pixels. This
learning process is expected to enable a smoother transition to
the noise filtering stage.
In Fig. 3, we illustrate the overview of the network structure
of MPM. The input to this module is network logits and
label maps. The module can be divided into two convolutional
blocks and a merging process. The first convolutional block is
designed to extract relationships between local features using
a single convolutional layer with a kernel size of 5, a stride
corresponding to the scale factor, and a Hyperbolic Tangent
activation function [50]. Following this, a merging process,
consisting of multiplication and summation operation, captures
the relationships between local features and labels, considering
label flipping similar to the approach of the Transition Matrix
[22]. Here, the Hyperbolic Tangent function produces values
in the range [−1, 1], ensuring that high-confidence values on
wrongly classified pixels are not ignored during the multipli-
cation operation with one-hot label vectors unlike the Softmax
function, which would yield values close to zero. The second
convolutional block aims to capture spatial relationships on
a larger scale. It includes two convolutional layers with a
kernel size of 3 to spatially smooth feature maps, followed
by a Sigmoid layer and an up-sampling layer to recover the
original size and produce the final masks.

on statistical measures of the mean and standard deviation,

D. Filtering Process to Loss function
To effectively filter out loss values on noisy pixels, we
introduce an LFM that guides the incorporation of filtering
masks into multi-loss functions. The “small-loss” trick [9]

is a common strategy for multi-class segmentation tasks. In
addition, we account for the existence of filtered-out pixels
by introducing CRF-Loss to the multi-loss to reuse the spatial
information of the input image, referencing previous WSSS
studies [33]. The CRF-Loss compensates for the insufficient
information in weakly annotated masks by facilitating interac-
tions between nearby pixels. Given the popularity of postpro-
cessing based on CRF, it intuitively seems to also be effective
for noisy information. However, transferring information from

IV. EXPERIMENTS
In this section, we evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed
method on two multi-class and one binary class classification
datasets. The first two datasets, DeepGlobe Landcover and
Mangrove Detection, are regarded as noisily annotated datasets
due to specific reasons. The DeepGlobe dataset is a coarsely
annotated public dataset used for a competition in 2018 [57],
and it has been noted to contain noisy pixels due to the
difficulty of landcover mapping [58]. The Mangrove dataset is
used for monitoring mangrove areas which play crucial roles
in coastal ecosystems. Previous research has pointed out the
difficulty of classification due to surrounding similar terrestrial
vegetation and changes in coastal areas due to periodic tides
[14], [15], resulting in the risk of wrongly annotated labels.
The last dataset is the Massachusetts dataset, which is a well-
used public dataset for building extraction and is not regarded
as noisy. However, we introduce artificial noise into the labels
to create a simulated noisy setting following Liu et al. [40].

1) Network dependency: The first experimental result, fo-

According to the table, it is evident that our proposed method

V. DISCUSSIONS
To further compare performance across methodologies, we
employ Cohen’s Kappa κ, ∆IoU, and the Top-3 mIoU for de-
tail model evaluation. Cohen’s Kappa is used to assess the con-
sistency between curators, while ∆IoU, and the Top-3 mIoU
measure the gap between the maximum and minimum class
IoU and assess the average in the top-3 class IoU, respectively,
where the class selection is based on the benchmark results.
The analysis results is summarized in table III.
Cohen’s Kappa has been mathematically analyzed in rela-
tion to the label noise distribution in datasets annotated by
multiple raters [64]. Because it is designed to subtract chance
agreement among curators, it is expected to mitigate distor-
tions in test evaluations due to noise, as discussed in detail
in Section VI. From Table III, it is evident that our proposed
method exhibits the highest kappa κ and demonstrates superior
correspondence to test labels compared to other methods.
Furthermore, upon comparing the mIoU evaluations in table II,
the rankings of methods in terms of mIoU align with the
kappa-based results, enhancing the reliability of the evaluation
in table II.
To further investigate the validity of kappa evaluation, we
created an additional test dataset with artificially introduced
noise, termed labeled masks with noise (LMN), along with
ground truth (GT) and calculate Cohen’s Kappa κ on the Mas-
sachusetts dataset, as shown in table IV. Due to the significant
proportion of random noise, κLMN showed a considerable score
decrease compared to κGT, thus we subtracted κGT (A) from
κLMN (B) and calculated B −A to assess the noise influence
for each method. Since the noise added to LMN does not vary
by method, if the evaluation based on kappa is noise-robust,
B −A is expected to be independent of the method. To test
this hypothesis, we calculated the statistical values of B −A
for each method as shown in Table IV , and confirm that the
standard deviation (0.0091) appears relatively small compared

The background of weak class preference in our method
stems from the two modules: MPM and NLPM. In MPM,
the initial convolution and multiplication with the label map
facilitate learning the relationships between classes, reflecting
flipping probabilities from prediction classes to label classes,
rather than solely depending on the difficulty of individual
classes. Additionaly, NLPM introduces noise regions for teach-

loss within the batch samples. Consequently, MPM is expected
to train to produce probabilities of extremely high loss on each
pixel, thereby suppressing the reflection of confidence levels
for each class and allowing focus solely on abnormal pixels.
Through the functionalities of these modules, our method
achieves a lower ∆IoU even compared to the benchmark,
indicating its capacity to reduce the risk of overfitting.

and β to highlight the challenges involved in tuning them.
Finally, we investigated the noise robustness of the kappa
coefficient as an evaluation metric through simple simulation
analyses.

To validate the use of Cohen’s kappa coefficient κ, we
next discuss its robustness to noise as an evaluation met-
ric. Cohen’s kappa κ subtracts the expected correct rate by
chance—commonly represented as Pe—thereby eliminating
contributions from random chance and promoting noise ro-
bustness. To validate this intuitive understanding, we conduct
a simple simulation where we assume that p% of labels have
been randomly flipped to one of the c classes. Assuming that
the labels are well class-balanced, the observed accuracy Po
and Cohen’s kappa κ on noisy labels can be related to the
clean accuracy Pcl and clean kappa κcl as follows:

In this formulation, the only difference between the two
metrics is the second term; therefore, we define the coefficients
for the clean metrics as c1 and c2, respectively, and calculate
the noise sensitivity as |c2/c1|. This ratio evaluates the extent
of noise dominance in each metric on noisy labels. The
simulated results in Fig. 9 show that when p ≈0, both
Po and κ closely match their clean counterparts, resulting
in |c2/c1| ≈0. However, as the noise rate p increases, the
accuracy Po becomes increasingly affected by noise, resulting
in the large value of |c2/c1|, whereas Cohen’s kappa κ remains
dependent solely on the clean terms, meaning |c2/c1| ≈0.
This simulation demonstrates that the formulation of Cohen’s
kappa effectively reduces the distortion caused by random
noise and helps preserve the ranking of different methods. In
real-world situations, noise can be more complex; however,
given the random nature of noise, Cohen’s kappa is one of the
more robust evaluation metrics, thereby making the evaluation
more reliable, supporting the discussion in SectionV.
VII. CONCLUSION
In this paper, we have introduced a method to handle noisy
labels in remote sensing image segmentation. This method
includes a co-training framework for reducing noise accumula-
tion, a filtering module to mitigate the impact of loss function
on uncertain pixels, and a weighted multi-loss for compen-
sating information by filtering operation. The experimental
results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method
across various datasets and network architectures. We observed
significant improvements in benchmark settings, particularly
with PSPNet, DeepLabV3+, and ST-UNet, indicating the ro-
bustness of our approach. Comparison with previous methods
revealed that our method outperforms others, with notable
improvements in accuracy and robustness. The analysis of
Cohen’s Kappa, ∆IoU, and Top-3 mIoU further supports
the reliability and noise-robustness of our evaluation metrics.
Our method’s capacity to reduce overfitting and its ability to
address weak class preferences highlight its effectiveness in
real-world applications.
Despite the adaptability of our method, certain aspects
remain unclear; the relationship between learning parameters
(or network structure) and the type of noise is not fully under-
stood. Furthermore, the potential of our method in scenarios
involving asymmetric networks, where the two networks differ
in their ability to extract features (e.g., receptive fields, feature
resolutions, or levels of abstraction), remains unexplored.
Addressing these gaps could be a promising direction for
future work to deepen our understanding and further improve
the efficacy of the proposed approach.
